strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the high computational cost and reproducibility barriers of search-based RL methods like AlphaZero in board games.

Proposes a simple, clear model-free algorithm (KLENT) that combines reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns, with a closed-form policy target derived in Appendix A and clear pseudocode in Algorithm 1.

Conducts extensive experiments across five board games plus 19x19 Go, with multiple baselines (AlphaZero, TRPO AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero, DQN, PPO) and an ablation study validating the three core components.

Provides substantial supplementary material: hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, bias-variance analysis for lambda-returns, head-to-head matches against Pachi/GnuGo, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., not superior asymptotic performance).
Reproducibility details are mostly provided: network architecture, optimizer, batch size, seeds, compute resources, and use of open-source Pgx/Mctx implementations.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method largely combines existing techniques (reverse KL + entropy regularization, lambda-returns), and the authors themselves state the novelty lies mainly in the empirical result rather than a new algorithmic principle.

Baseline tuning is insufficient and potentially unfair in the main comparisons. The main experiments use AlphaZero with 32 MCTS rollouts, but Appendix G.1 shows 8 rollouts is far better in 9x9 Go (e.g., 69% vs 34% win rate at 800M simulator evaluations). The strongest tuned AlphaZero baseline is not included in the main figures, which may overstate KLENT's efficiency advantage.

Gumbel AlphaZero is also not tuned per environment in the main experiments, and its reported performance in 9x9 Go appears weaker than the tuned AlphaZero(8) from Appendix G.1, raising concerns that the main search-based baseline is suboptimal.
Evaluation against a fixed anchored opponent can saturate (e.g., 90-100% win rates in several games), which limits discriminative power and does not fully establish absolute playing strength.

The 'simulator evaluations' metric may not fully capture computational differences between search-based and model-free methods (e.g., MCTS tree traversal overhead, memory usage, and the large disparity in number of training samples per simulator evaluation).
No code release is mentioned, which limits full reproducibility despite the detailed appendices.
The claim of more efficient learning is less convincing in Animal Shogi and Gardner Chess, where differences from search-based methods are small and sometimes within variance.
The method lacks theoretical convergence or stability analysis; its behavior relies primarily on empirical ablation.

strengths: Proposes KLENT, a model-free RL algorithm combining reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns with a closed-form policy improvement target.

Conducts experiments on five board games and 19x19 Go, including ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity, bias-variance analysis of lambda-returns, convergence to quantal response equilibrium, and head-to-head matches against GnuGo/Pachi.
Uses open-source implementations (Pgx, Mctx) and pretrained checkpoints, with detailed hyperparameters and implementation descriptions.
Includes an honest limitations discussion regarding asymptotic performance and provides computational requirements.
Writing is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a combination of existing techniques (MPO-style reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, lambda-returns, direct action-value modeling) with a standard closed-form solution; no new theoretical insight. The authors acknowledge the novelty lies mainly in empirical results.

Unfair baseline configuration: main experiments use a fixed MCTS budget of 32 simulations per move for all search-based methods. Appendix G shows AlphaZero performs much better with 8 rollouts in 9x9 Go and 16 in 19x19 Go, but these tuned settings are not used in the main comparison, and Gumbel AlphaZero is not tuned at all. This inflates KLENT's apparent efficiency.

The primary metric (simulator evaluations) ignores training compute. For the same simulator evaluations, KLENT performs many more gradient updates than search-based methods (e.g., roughly 32x more in 9x9 Go with 32 MCTS simulations), so total compute is not equal. The paper reports only a modest 25% wall-clock reduction in one environment (Appendix K), which conflicts with the claimed 'fourfold efficiency gain' based on simulator evaluations.

Evaluation against a single anchored opponent may not reflect true relative strength. The main comparisons do not include direct head-to-head matches between KLENT and Gumbel AlphaZero in the five games. The 19x19 head-to-head is only against AlphaZero and uses a different network (20 blocks) and opponent (ElfOpenGo), making it not directly comparable to the five-game results.
Experimental setup differences may confound efficiency comparisons: model-free methods use up to 2048 state transitions per thread while search-based methods use up to 256, without justification.
No code release for KLENT is mentioned, limiting reproducibility despite detailed descriptions.
Reference and formatting errors are present (e.g., 'Bellman (2005)' for a 1957 paper, 'D Richard Delorme', inconsistent years for Silver et al.).

The central claim that KLENT achieves more efficient learning than existing methods is not adequately supported due to the above issues, especially the unfair baseline tuning and the metric that ignores training cost.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper tackles the high computational cost and reproducibility barrier of search-based RL in board games by asking whether look-ahead search can be entirely eliminated during training.

Simple, well-founded method: KLENT combines reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns; the closed-form policy improvement solution is derived correctly and the direct action-value network removes the need for MCTS.

Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation: five board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) with comparisons to AlphaZero, TRPO AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero, DQN, and PPO. KLENT achieves substantial efficiency gains, e.g., reaching 50% average win rate with 75M simulator evaluations versus 300M for Gumbel AlphaZero.

Thorough ablation study: KL Only, ENT Only, 1-Step KLENT, and Monte Carlo KLENT isolate the contributions of KL regularization, entropy regularization, and intermediate lambda-returns; entropy evolution analysis further supports the claims.

Good scalability and test-time analysis: KLENT is competitive with AlphaZero on 19x19 Go, scales with additional test-time MCTS, and wins head-to-head matches against GnuGo, Pachi, and AlphaZero checkpoints in appendix experiments.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: detailed network architecture, hyperparameters, optimizer settings, parallel self-play protocol, libraries (Pgx, Mctx, Stable-Baselines3), random seeds, and sensitivity analysis are provided. Limitations are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: the three core components (reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, lambda-returns) are existing techniques, and the closed-form solution is a known result for this regularized objective. The main contribution is empirical rather than theoretical.

Baseline tuning concerns: the main experiments use AlphaZero with 32 MCTS simulations, but Appendix G shows 8 simulations is more efficient in 9x9 Go. Thus the AlphaZero comparison may be suboptimal. However, the central claim still holds because KLENT also outperforms tuned AlphaZero(8) and Gumbel AlphaZero.

Computational-cost metric is imperfect: 'simulator evaluations' is a useful proxy but does not fully capture wall-clock cost differences from neural network forward/backward passes and parameter updates. Training wall-clock comparisons are limited (e.g., only a >25% reduction reported for 9x9 Go), while test-time wall-clock is measured more carefully.

Evaluation relies heavily on win rates against a single anchored Pgx baseline. Although additional head-to-head and Elo results are provided in appendices, broader round-robin or diverse opponent evaluation would more robustly establish playing strength.
No code release is mentioned. While implementation details are detailed, exact reproduction may still require nontrivial effort in integrating Pgx/Mctx, parallel self-play, and the on-policy buffer.

Minor presentation and reference issues: e.g., 'Solot et al.' vs 'Sokota et al.', 'Wirig', 'Bellman (2005)' for a 1957 reference, and some low-resolution figures. The distinction between reactive-policy evaluation and fixed test-time simulation budgets could also be stated more clearly.

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical contribution: KLENT is evaluated on five board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) plus large-scale 19x19 Go, with up to ~4x simulator-evaluation efficiency over Gumbel AlphaZero and strong head-to-head win rates (e.g., 89% on 9x9 Go, 98% on Hex), supported by extensive appendices (sensitivity analysis, architecture ablations, baseline reliability checks, test-time scaling, wall-clock comparisons).

The ablation study cleanly isolates each design component: removing reverse-KL regularization (ENT Only) causes abrupt policy updates (Figure 8), removing entropy regularization (KL Only) collapses entropy and destabilizes learning (Figure 9), and replacing λ-returns degrades performance, giving a coherent mechanistic story.

The normal-form game analysis (Theorem C.8 / Corollary C.9) is rigorous, based on a clean Jacobian/operator-norm contraction argument with a weighted norm, and yields a strictly broader convergence region than Sokota et al. (2022), which is verified numerically in Figure 3 where the empirical convergence/divergence boundary matches the theoretical condition.

The paper is honest about its scope: it explicitly states that the contributions are new theoretical/empirical characterizations rather than new algorithmic ingredients, and the limitations section candidly acknowledges the efficiency (rather than asymptotic-performance) focus.
Reproducibility is reasonable: open-source baselines (Pgx/Mctx), unified network architecture, disclosed hyperparameters, and reported compute budget (~2000 A100 GPU-hours).

Practical significance: demonstrating that a pure model-free method can eliminate MCTS while remaining competitive/efficient in board games is useful for resource-constrained settings and connects to discrete optimization and reasoning domains.
weaknesses: The finite-length game 'convergence guarantee' (Theorem C.12) is informal. The proof assumes Q_θ has already converged to a fixed Q^π and analyzes a logit recurrence treating the value target as fixed; it does not rigorously handle the coupled two-timescale dynamics of simultaneous policy and value updates, nor the bootstrapping interaction between Q_θ and the evolving policy. This weakens one of the two headline theoretical claims.

Novelty is incremental: the algorithmic combination (reverse-KL + entropy regularization) is essentially known (MPO/V-MPO, Sokota et al.), and the authors acknowledge this. The theoretical gain over prior work is a constant-factor broadening of the convergence condition obtained via a looser bound (Lemma C.6/Popoviciu).

The comparison of the convergence condition to Sokota et al. (2022) (αβ > ||R||²) is not fully justified as apples-to-apples; the paper does not demonstrate that the update rule and parametrization analyzed there are identical, so the claimed 'broader coverage' could be an artifact of differing analysis assumptions.

Baseline strength is a concern: AlphaZero is reported at only 7% (32 rollouts) and even tuned to 8 rollouts reaches 69% at 800M, while KLENT reaches 89%. Although Appendix K/L make a good-faith effort to validate the Pgx implementation and tune rollouts, the simulator-evaluation metric counts environment steps but not the per-node neural-network inference cost of MCTS, which could bias the efficiency comparison (only partially addressed by the wall-clock table in Appendix M).

Evaluation relies primarily on win rate against a single fixed anchored opponent, a proxy susceptible to non-transitivity; Elo is relegated to an appendix with the caveat that it is unreliable, leaving strength assessment somewhat narrow.
Introductory claims that KLENT may accelerate real-world domains such as discrete optimization, algorithmic discovery, and mathematical proving are speculative and untested in this work.

strengths: The paper revisits an interesting and practically relevant combination of reverse KL regularization and entropy regularization, providing a closed-form policy update and a practical model-free algorithm (KLENT) for board games.

The normal-form game analysis (Theorem C.8/Corollary C.9) gives a sufficient condition for local linear convergence, α(α+2β) > ||R||_2^2/4, which is broader than the previously reported condition αβ > ||R||_2^2 from Sokota et al. (2022); the proof via Jacobian spectral radius is technically sound for that setting.

The empirical study is extensive, covering five board games and 19x19 Go, and includes ablations for KL regularization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns that help isolate the contribution of each component.
The paper provides a reasonably detailed experimental setup, hyperparameters, and implementation notes, and uses open-source libraries (Pgx, Mctx), which aids reproducibility.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges that the work focuses on training efficiency rather than asymptotic performance with unlimited compute.
weaknesses: The finite-length game theorem (Theorem C.12) is not rigorous. The proof assumes Q_theta converges to Q^π and then analyzes a logit recurrence, but it does not account for function approximation, replay buffers, λ-returns, or the coupled, non-stationary self-play dynamics of two-player zero-sum games. It effectively analyzes an idealized single-agent MDP rather than the practical KLENT algorithm.

The Count Up Game, used as the only empirical verification of the finite-length theorem, is not correctly formalized as a two-player game. The state is just the cumulative sum, the transition only includes the current player's action (S_{t+1}=S_t+A_t), and the state does not encode whose turn it is. This reduces the testbed to a single-player subtraction game, so it does not validate the claimed two-player zero-sum convergence result.

The main experimental comparison uses search-based baselines with a fixed 32 MCTS simulations per action, but Appendix L shows that 8 rollouts are substantially more efficient for AlphaZero in 9x9 Go. The main figures do not use these tuned baselines, which may overstate KLENT's efficiency advantage. Gumbel AlphaZero is similarly not tuned per environment.

The headline claim of 'up to 4x higher training efficiency' is based on simulator evaluations, not wall-clock time. Appendix P reports only a >25% wall-clock improvement in 9x9 Go, so the abstract and introduction overstate the practical efficiency gain.

Novelty is limited. The combination of reverse KL and entropy regularization has been studied before (Vieillard et al., 2020a; Sokota et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2023), and the authors explicitly state that their main contributions are not new algorithmic ingredients. The theoretical improvement in normal-form games is incremental, and the empirical gains are domain-specific.

Evaluation against a fixed anchored opponent may not reflect true strength against the trained baselines. Head-to-head matches are limited to a single 19x19 Go setting in Appendix N.2 and are not systematically reported across the five board games.

The paper claims applicability to 'an MDP with a finite action space,' but two-player zero-sum games are not standard MDPs because transitions depend on the opponent's actions. The mismatch between the single-agent MDP perspective and the two-player self-play setting is not adequately addressed in the theory or experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly framed question: whether a pure model-free algorithm can learn board games stably and efficiently without look-ahead search. The motivation (reducing the massive compute of AlphaZero-style methods) is important and timely.

It provides novel theoretical results: a convergence condition α(α+2β) > ||R||²/4 for normal-form games that strictly broadens the region covered by Sokota et al. (2022) (αβ > ||R||²), verified numerically on Matching Pennies, plus a finite-length game convergence analysis tied to the entropy-regularized (quantal response) equilibrium and validated on the Count Up Game.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive and convincing: five board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) plus 19x19 Go, with search-based (AlphaZero, TRPO-AZ, Gumbel-AZ) and model-free (DQN, PPO) baselines, ablations of all three components (KL, entropy, λ-returns), test-time MCTS scaling, head-to-head and external-engine matches (GnuGo, Pachi), and Elo reference curves.

The claimed 4x efficiency gain is supported by multiple analyses, and the ablation study cleanly isolates the effect of each ingredient (e.g., the entropy collapse in KL-Only and the elevated KL divergence in ENT-Only).
Reproducibility is good: open-source Pgx/Mctx frameworks, a single A100 for KLENT, reported compute budget (~2000 GPU-hours total), and detailed hyperparameter/architecture tables.

The limitations section is honest and does not overclaim asymptotic superiority over search-based methods, and the appendix preemptively addresses likely reviewer concerns (rollout-count tuning, architecture comparison, baseline reliability).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: the method is essentially a known combination of reverse-KL and entropy regularization (Vieillard et al., 2020a; Sokota et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2023), which the authors explicitly acknowledge. The theoretical results are also incremental extensions of Sokota et al. (2022).

The finite-length game theorem (C.12) has proof gaps: it assumes the action-value estimate has converged before deriving policy convergence, without rigorously establishing joint (policy/value) convergence or a rate—the backward-induction argument is somewhat heuristic.
Theorem 5.1 asserts convergence to 'the unique fixed point' without justifying uniqueness; quantal-response/regularized equilibria are not generally unique, so this claim needs support.

The primary comparison metric (number of simulator evaluations) structurally favors model-free methods, since each MCTS evaluation is a single environment interaction but search-based methods spend many evaluations per decision. Training wall-clock/FLOPs are not systematically reported (only a vague '>25%' claim in one setting), which weakens the efficiency argument.

There is an inconsistency between the main experiments and the appendix: the main results use 32 rollouts per action for AlphaZero, while Appendix L shows 8 rollouts is optimal for 9x9 Go. Using a sub-optimal setting in the headline figure may overstate the reported gap, even though the appendix shows KLENT still wins under tuned settings.

The key comparison rests on the AlphaZero-family implementation; DQN/PPO are weak, non-representative baselines for board games, and the strength of the Pgx anchored opponent (while defended in Appendix K) determines much of the reported win rates.
